reminder: An irrational number is a real number that is not a quotient of two integers.
definition: A [real number](c:real-number) $x$ is irrational when it is not a [rational number](c:rational-number), so no [integers](c:integer) $p$ and $q\neq 0$ satisfy $x=p/q$. Equivalently, its decimal expansion never ends and never repeats.
examples: $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. If $\sqrt2=p/q$ in lowest terms, then $p^2=2q^2$ makes $p$ and $q$ both even, which is a contradiction.
The numbers $\pi$ and $e$ are irrational.
Non-example: $0.333\ldots=1/3$ is rational, because its decimal expansion repeats.

steps: Start with the set of [real numbers](c:real-number).
Remove every [rational number](c:rational-number) from this set.
The numbers that remain are the irrational numbers, so each irrational number is a real number with one extra condition.
links.why: It shows that irrationality is a property of real numbers: you test a real number against the rationals.

steps: Take an irrational number $x$.
Add the condition that $x$ solves $ax^2+bx+c=0$ for some integers $a$, $b$, $c$ with $a\neq 0$.
The irrational numbers with this extra condition are the quadratic irrational numbers, for example $\sqrt2$.
links.why: It tells you that every quadratic irrational number is irrational, so results on irrational numbers apply to it.

reminder: The limit of $f$ at $a$ is the value $L$ that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ approaches $a$.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f$ of a [real number](c:real-number) and a point $a$, we write $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that $0<|x-a|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. More generally, $f$ tends to $L$ along a [filter](c:filter) when the preimage of every [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) of $L$ belongs to the filter.
examples: $\lim_{x\to 2}(3x+1)=7$: for a given $\varepsilon$, the choice $\delta=\varepsilon/3$ works.
$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$, although the quotient has no value at $0$.
Non-example: $\lim_{x\to 0}\sin(1/x)$ does not exist, because the values keep oscillating between $-1$ and $1$.

steps: Take the [filter](c:filter) of punctured neighbourhoods of $a$.
Push this filter forward along $f$ to get a filter on the target.
The value $L$ is the limit of $f$ at $a$ exactly when this pushed filter converges to $L$.
links.why: It shows that limits of functions, limits of sequences and limits at infinity are one idea with different filters.

steps: Take a point $a$ in the domain of $f$.
Ask that the limit of $f$ at $a$ exists and equals the value $f(a)$.
A function with this property at every point is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
links.why: It shows that continuity is the special case of a limit where the limit equals the value of the function.

reminder: A function is lower semicontinuous at $x$ when the values at nearby points are not much lower than $f(x)$.
definition: A function $f$ from a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ to the [real numbers](c:real-number) (or to $\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$) is lower semicontinuous when at every point $x$ the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior) of $f(y)$ as $y\to x$ is at least $f(x)$. Equivalently, for every real number $t$ the set $\{x: f(x)>t\}$ is an [open set](c:open-set).
examples: Every continuous real function is lower semicontinuous.
The indicator function of an open set $U$ is lower semicontinuous: each set $\{f>t\}$ is empty, equal to $U$, or the whole space.
Non-example: the indicator function of $\{0\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not lower semicontinuous, because $\{f>0\}=\{0\}$ is not open.

steps: Take a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f$ on a topological space and a real number $t$.
The set $\{f>t\}$ is the preimage of the open interval $(t,\infty)$, so it is open.
Hence $f$ is lower semicontinuous, but continuity also asks that every set $\{f<t\}$ is open.
links.why: It shows that results for lower semicontinuous functions cover all continuous functions, and that one half of continuity is enough for them.

reminder: A Markov chain is a random process in which the next state depends only on the current state.
definition: A Markov chain is a sequence of [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_0,X_1,\dots$ with values in a set of states (a discrete-time [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process)) such that $P(X_{n+1}=y\mid X_0,\dots,X_n)=P(X_{n+1}=y\mid X_n)$. For a time-homogeneous chain, the [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) $p(x,y)=P(X_{n+1}=y\mid X_n=x)$ gives the transition probabilities.
examples: A simple random walk on the integers: each step adds $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $1/2$, whatever the past is.
A weather model with states sunny and rainy, where tomorrow depends only on today through fixed transition probabilities.
Non-example: draw cards from a deck without replacement and let $X_n$ be the $n$-th card. The law of $X_{n+1}$ depends on all earlier cards, not only on $X_n$.

steps: Take a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_n)$ with a countable set of states.
Add the Markov property: given $X_n$, the future of the process is independent of its past.
The process is then a Markov chain, and its law is fixed by the initial law and the transition probabilities.
links.why: It shows that a Markov chain is a stochastic process with one memory condition, so general process results apply to it.

reminder: The orthogonal projection onto a subspace sends each vector to the nearest point of that subspace.
definition: Let $H$ be an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) and $M$ a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) such that every vector has a nearest point in $M$ (this holds when $M$ is finite dimensional, or closed in a Hilbert space). The orthogonal projection onto $M$ is the [linear map](c:linear-map) $P$ that sends $x$ to the unique $Px\in M$ with $x-Px$ [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) to $M$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, projection onto the $x$-axis sends $(a,b)$ to $(a,0)$.
In $\mathbb{R}^n$, projection onto the line through a unit vector $u$ sends $x$ to $\langle x,u\rangle u$.
Non-example: the map $(a,b)\mapsto(a+b,0)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $P^2=P$ and has image the $x$-axis, but it is not orthogonal, because $(a,b)-P(a,b)=(-b,b)$ is not orthogonal to the $x$-axis.

steps: A [projection operator](c:projection-operator) is a linear map $P$ with $P^2=P$.
The orthogonal projection $P_M$ fixes every point of $M$ and has image $M$, so $P_M^2=P_M$.
The extra condition for an orthogonal projection is that the kernel of $P_M$ is orthogonal to its image $M$.
links.why: It shows that an orthogonal projection is a projection with the best choice of kernel, so idempotent facts apply to it.

reminder: A prime ideal is a proper ideal $P$ such that $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$.
definition: An [ideal](c:ideal) $P$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is prime when $P\neq R$ and $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. Equivalently, the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $R/P$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, the ideal $(n)$ with $n\ge0$ is prime exactly when $n=0$ or $n$ is a prime number.
In $k[x,y]$ over a field $k$, the ideal $(x)$ is prime, because the quotient $k[x,y]/(x)\cong k[y]$ is an integral domain.
Non-example: $(6)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ is not prime, because $2\cdot 3\in(6)$ but neither $2$ nor $3$ lies in $(6)$.

steps: Take an [ideal](c:ideal) $P$ of a commutative ring $R$.
Require that $P$ is a proper ideal, so $P\neq R$.
Require that $ab\in P$ forces $a\in P$ or $b\in P$; then $P$ is a prime ideal.
links.why: It shows that a prime ideal is an ordinary ideal with a divisibility condition, so ideal operations apply to it.

steps: Let $M$ be a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) of a commutative ring $R$.
The quotient ring $R/M$ is a field.
A field is an integral domain, so $M$ is a prime ideal.
links.why: It tells you that every maximal ideal is prime, but a prime ideal such as $(0)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ need not be maximal.

steps: Let $p$ be a [prime element](c:prime-element) of a commutative ring $R$: a nonunit such that $p\mid ab$ implies $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$.
Pass to the principal ideal $(p)$, where membership in $(p)$ means divisibility by $p$.
Then $ab\in(p)$ implies $a\in(p)$ or $b\in(p)$, so $(p)$ is a prime ideal.
links.why: It turns the divisibility property of prime numbers into a property of ideals, which also works in rings without unique factorization.

reminder: The q-expansion writes a modular form as a power series in $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$.
definition: A [modular form](c:modular-form) $f$ of level 1 satisfies $f(\tau+1)=f(\tau)$ on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane), so it is a function of $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$ and has a [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) $f(\tau)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nq^n$. This series is the q-expansion of $f$ at the [cusp](c:cusp) $\infty$. At a cusp of width $h$ for a form of higher level, one uses $q^{1/h}$ instead of $q$.
examples: The Eisenstein series $E_4$ has the q-expansion $1+240\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_3(n)q^n$.
The discriminant form $\Delta=q-24q^2+252q^3-\cdots$ has a q-expansion that starts at $n=1$.
Non-example: the function $f(\tau)=\tau$ on the upper half plane has no q-expansion, because $f(\tau+1)\neq f(\tau)$ and so $f$ is not a function of $q$.

steps: A [modular form](c:modular-form) $f$ has period 1, so $f(\tau)$ is a periodic function of the real part of $\tau$.
Expand it as the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) $\sum_n a_n e^{2\pi i n\tau}$.
Holomorphy at the cusp removes every term with $n<0$, and what remains is the q-expansion.
links.why: It shows that a q-expansion is an ordinary Fourier series, so facts on Fourier coefficients apply to it.

reminder: In a regular space, each point and each closed set that misses it have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is regular when for every point $x$ and every [closed set](c:closed-set) $C$ with $x\notin C$ there are disjoint [open sets](c:open-set) $U$ and $V$ with $x\in U$ and $C\subseteq V$. Many authors call a space regular only when it is also a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
examples: Every metric space is regular.
Every compact Hausdorff space is regular.

Non-example: the Sierpiński space $\{0,1\}$ with open sets $\emptyset$, $\{1\}$, $\{0,1\}$ is not regular. The point $1$ and the closed set $\{0\}$ cannot be separated, because the only open set that contains $0$ is the whole space.

steps: Start with a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$.
Take a point $x$ and a closed set $C$ that does not contain $x$.
Require disjoint open sets around $x$ and around $C$ for every such pair; then $X$ is regular.
links.why: It shows that regularity is a separation condition added to a general topology.

steps: Let $X$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space) with its metric topology, and take a point $x$ and a closed set $C$ with $x\notin C$.
Since $C$ is closed, $r=d(x,C)$ is positive.
The open sets $\{y: d(y,x)<r/2\}$ and $\{y: d(y,C)<r/2\}$ are disjoint, so $X$ is regular.
links.why: It tells you that every metric space is regular, so metric spaces satisfy results that need regularity.

reminder: Sheaf cohomology measures how far taking global sections is from being exact on a sheaf.
definition: For a [sheaf](c:sheaf) $F$ of abelian groups on a space $X$, the sheaf cohomology groups $H^n(X,F)$ are the right [derived functors](c:derived-functor) of the functor $F\mapsto F(X)$ of [global sections](c:global-section). Concretely, choose an injective resolution $0\to F\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ and take the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the complex $I^0(X)\to I^1(X)\to\cdots$.
examples: $H^0(X,F)=F(X)$ is the group of global sections of $F$.
For a smooth manifold $X$ and the constant sheaf $\mathbb{R}$, $H^n(X,\mathbb{R})$ is the [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology) of $X$.

Non-example: the [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) of one fixed open cover is not sheaf cohomology in general. The two agree when the sheaf has no higher cohomology on the finite intersections of the cover (Leray).

steps: Take an injective resolution $I^\bullet$ of the [sheaf](c:sheaf) $F$.
Apply the functor of global sections to get a cochain complex $I^\bullet(X)$ of abelian groups.
The [cohomology](c:cohomology) of this complex is $H^n(X,F)$, so sheaf cohomology is the cohomology of one special cochain complex.
links.why: It shows that sheaf cohomology obeys the general rules of cohomology, such as long exact sequences.

steps: Let $X$ be a smooth manifold, whose sheaves of smooth $p$-forms are fine and have no higher sheaf cohomology.
The Poincaré lemma makes $0\to\mathbb{R}\to\Omega^0\to\Omega^1\to\cdots$ an exact sequence of sheaves.
Hence $H^n(X,\mathbb{R})$ equals the cohomology of the complex of global forms, which is de Rham cohomology.
links.why: It tells you that de Rham cohomology is sheaf cohomology of the constant sheaf, so sheaf tools compute it.

reminder: The tensor product $V\otimes W$ turns bilinear maps out of $V\times W$ into linear maps out of $V\otimes W$.
definition: For [modules](c:module) $V$ and $W$ over a commutative ring (for example [vector spaces](c:vector-space) over a field), the tensor product is a module $V\otimes W$ with a [bilinear map](c:bilinear-map) $V\times W\to V\otimes W$, $(v,w)\mapsto v\otimes w$. It has this [universal property](c:universal-property): every bilinear map $b:V\times W\to U$ equals $g\circ\otimes$ for exactly one [linear map](c:linear-map) $g:V\otimes W\to U$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^m\otimes\mathbb{R}^n\cong\mathbb{R}^{mn}$, with basis $e_i\otimes f_j$.
$\mathbb{Z}/2\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}/3=0$, because each $a\otimes b$ is killed by both $2$ and $3$.
Non-example: the direct product $V\times W$ is not $V\otimes W$. For $\dim V=m$ and $\dim W=n$ it has dimension $m+n$, not $mn$.

steps: Take the ring $R=\mathbb{Z}$.
Every abelian group is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, and every group homomorphism is $\mathbb{Z}$-linear.
A $\mathbb{Z}$-bilinear map is a map that is additive in each variable, so the module tensor product is the tensor product of abelian groups.
links.why: It shows that the tensor product of abelian groups is the case $R=\mathbb{Z}$ of the tensor product of modules.

steps: Let $A$ and $B$ be algebras over a commutative ring $R$, so both are $R$-modules.
Form the module $A\otimes_R B$.
Define $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$; this gives the tensor product of algebras.
links.why: It shows that the tensor product of algebras is the module tensor product with one extra multiplication.

reminder: A transcendental number is a complex number that is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients.
definition: A [complex number](c:complex-number) $z$ is transcendental when it is not an [algebraic number](c:algebraic-number): no nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) with rational coefficients has $z$ as a [root](c:root). Equivalently, $z$ is not algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$.
examples: $\pi$ and $e$ are transcendental (Lindemann for $\pi$, Hermite for $e$).
Liouville's constant $\sum_{n\ge1}10^{-n!}$ is transcendental.
Non-example: $\sqrt2$ is algebraic, because it is a root of $x^2-2$.

steps: Suppose $z=p/q$ is rational with $q\neq 0$.
Then $z$ is a root of the nonzero polynomial $qx-p$ with rational coefficients, so $z$ is algebraic.
By contraposition, a transcendental number is not rational, so a transcendental real number is [irrational](c:irrational-number).
links.why: It tells you that transcendence is stronger than irrationality: $\sqrt2$ is irrational but not transcendental.

reminder: The Wightman axioms define a quantum field theory as fields on a Hilbert space with covariance, positive energy, locality and a cyclic vacuum.
definition: A Wightman theory on [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) consists of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\mathcal H$ with a [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) of the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group), a vacuum vector $\Omega$, and [operator-valued distributions](c:operator-valued-distribution) $\phi_i$ on a dense domain that contains $\Omega$. The axioms require that the energy-momentum spectrum lies in the closed forward light cone, that $\Omega$ is the unique invariant vector up to a scalar, that the fields transform covariantly, that fields at spacelike separation commute (or anticommute for fermions), and that $\Omega$ is cyclic for the fields.
examples: The free scalar field of positive mass in four spacetime dimensions satisfies the axioms.
The $P(\varphi)_2$ models in two spacetime dimensions satisfy the axioms, by the work of Glimm and Jaffe.
Non-example: a theory with an indefinite inner product, as in covariant-gauge quantum electrodynamics, has no Hilbert space of states and so does not satisfy the axioms in this form.

reminder: A 3-manifold is a space that looks like ordinary three-dimensional space near every point.
definition: A 3-manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) of dimension 3: a Hausdorff, second-countable [topological space](c:topological-space) in which every point has a neighbourhood [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
examples: The 3-sphere $S^3$ and the 3-torus $S^1\times S^1\times S^1$.
The space $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the complement of a knot in $S^3$.
Non-example: the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a 2-manifold, not a 3-manifold, because no point of it has a neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

steps: Start with a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ and its dimension $n$, which does not depend on the chart.
Require $n=3$, so that every chart goes to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
The manifolds with this extra condition are the 3-manifolds.
links.why: It shows that general manifold results apply to 3-manifolds, which add only the dimension condition.

steps: A [hyperbolic 3-manifold](c:hyperbolic-3-manifold) is a 3-manifold $M$ with a complete Riemannian metric of constant curvature $-1$.
Forget the metric and keep only the topological space $M$.
What remains is a 3-manifold, so every hyperbolic 3-manifold is a 3-manifold.
links.why: It shows that hyperbolic 3-manifolds are the 3-manifolds with an extra geometric structure.

reminder: An antiderivative of $f$ is a function $F$ whose derivative equals $f$.
definition: Let $f$ be a [function](c:function) on an [interval](c:interval). An antiderivative of $f$ is a [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $F$ on the interval with $F'(x)=f(x)$ at every point $x$, where $F'$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) of $F$. Two antiderivatives of $f$ on an interval differ by a constant.
examples: $F(x)=x^3/3$ is an antiderivative of $x^2$, and so is $x^3/3+5$.
If $f$ is continuous, then $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ is an antiderivative of $f$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Non-example: the sign function has no antiderivative on $\mathbb{R}$. The function $|x|$ has derivative $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ only away from $0$, and a derivative cannot have a jump (Darboux property).

reminder: An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which each term is the previous term plus a fixed difference.
definition: An arithmetic progression is a [sequence](c:sequence) of [integers](c:integer) or [real numbers](c:real-number) $a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\dots$ in which each term exceeds the previous term by the same constant $d$. The number $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference; a finite progression of length $k$ ends at $a+(k-1)d$.
examples: $3,7,11,15$ has first term $a=3$ and common difference $d=4$.
The primes $5,11,17,23,29$ form an arithmetic progression with $d=6$.
Non-example: $1,2,4,8$ is not an arithmetic progression, because the differences $1,2,4$ are not equal.

steps: Take a [sequence](c:sequence) $(x_n)$ of numbers.
Add the condition that $x_{n+1}-x_n$ has the same value $d$ for every $n$.
Then $x_n=x_0+nd$, so the sequence is an arithmetic progression.
links.why: It shows that an arithmetic progression is a sequence with one constancy condition, and it gives the closed formula for its terms.

steps: A [generalized arithmetic progression](c:generalized-arithmetic-progression) is a set $\{a+n_1d_1+\dots+n_rd_r : 0\le n_i<N_i\}$.
Take the rank $r=1$.
The set becomes $\{a,\,a+d_1,\dots,a+(N_1-1)d_1\}$, a finite arithmetic progression.
links.why: It shows that an arithmetic progression is a generalized progression of rank one.

reminder: A Borel set is a set that you can build from open sets by countable unions and complements.
definition: In a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$, the Borel sets are the members of the smallest [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) that contains every [open set](c:open-set). So you obtain each Borel set from open sets by taking complements and countable unions, possibly transfinitely many times.
examples: Every open set and every closed set of $\mathbb{R}$ is Borel, and so is every countable set.
The set of irrational numbers is Borel, because it is a countable intersection of open sets.
Non-example: a Vitali set (one point from each coset of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $[0,1]$) is not Lebesgue measurable, so it is not Borel.

steps: Give the space $X$ its Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B$, the smallest one that contains the open sets.
Then $(X,\mathcal B)$ is a [measurable space](c:measurable-space).
The measurable sets of this space are exactly the Borel sets.
links.why: It shows that a Borel set is a measurable set for the sigma-algebra that the topology generates.

steps: Take an [open set](c:open-set) $U$ of $X$.
The Borel sigma-algebra contains every open set by definition, so $U$ is a Borel set.
Closed sets are Borel too, because a sigma-algebra contains complements.
links.why: It shows that open and closed sets are the first Borel sets from which all others are built.

reminder: A function is concave when the chord between two points of its graph lies on or below the graph.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:C\to\mathbb{R}$ on a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$ is concave when $f(tx+(1-t)y)\ge tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and all $t\in[0,1]$. Equivalently, $-f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function).
examples: $\log x$ on $(0,\infty)$ and $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ are concave.
Every affine function is concave, and it is also convex.
Non-example: $x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not concave. For $x=0$, $y=2$ and $t=1/2$ we get $f(1)=1$, which is less than $\tfrac12 f(0)+\tfrac12 f(2)=2$.

reminder: The conjugacy class of $g$ is the set of all elements $hgh^{-1}$ with $h$ in the group.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $g\in G$. The conjugacy class of $g$ is the set $\{hgh^{-1} : h\in G\}$, which is the [orbit](c:orbit) of $g$ under the action of $G$ on itself by [conjugation](c:conjugation). The conjugacy classes partition $G$.
examples: In $S_3$ the classes are the identity, the three transpositions and the two 3-cycles.
In an abelian group every class has exactly one element.
Non-example: in $S_3$ the set $\{(12),(13)\}$ is not a conjugacy class. Conjugating $(12)$ by $(123)$ gives $(23)$, which is not in the set.

steps: Let $G$ act on itself by $h\cdot x=hxh^{-1}$.
This rule is a [group action](c:group-action): $(hk)\cdot x=h\cdot(k\cdot x)$ and $e\cdot x=x$.
The [orbit](c:orbit) of $g$ under this action is $\{hgh^{-1}\}$, the conjugacy class of $g$.
links.why: It shows that conjugacy classes inherit orbit facts, such as partitioning the group and the orbit-stabilizer count.

reminder: A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior in Euclidean space.
definition: A convex body in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a subset $K$ that is a [convex set](c:convex-set) (the segment between any two points of $K$ lies in $K$), is [compact](c:compact-space), and has nonempty [interior](c:interior).
examples: The closed unit ball and the cube $[0,1]^n$ are convex bodies.
A closed triangle in the plane is a convex body, and so is every convex polytope with nonempty interior.
Non-example: a closed line segment in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is convex and compact, but its interior is empty.
Non-example: the open unit ball is convex with nonempty interior, but it is not compact.

steps: Take a [convex set](c:convex-set) $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Add the condition that $K$ is closed and bounded, so $K$ is compact.
Add the condition that $K$ contains an open ball; then $K$ is a convex body.
links.why: It shows that a convex body is a convex set with two size conditions, so convexity results apply to it.

steps: Take a [convex polytope](c:convex-polytope) $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, the convex hull of finitely many points.
The set $P$ is convex, and it is compact because it is the continuous image of a simplex.
If $P$ has nonempty interior, it is a convex body, so convex bodies include all full-dimensional polytopes.
links.why: It shows that polytopes give many concrete convex bodies, and convex bodies also include round shapes such as balls.

reminder: A cusp form is a modular form whose Fourier expansion vanishes at every cusp.
definition: A cusp form is a [modular form](c:modular-form) that vanishes at every [cusp](c:cusp). For level 1, this means that the constant coefficient $a_0$ of its [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nq^n$ is zero.
examples: The discriminant $\Delta=q\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n)^{24}$ is a cusp form of weight 12 and level 1.
The cusp forms of weight 12 and level 1 are exactly the scalar multiples of $\Delta$.
Non-example: the Eisenstein series $E_4=1+240q+\cdots$ is a modular form with $a_0=1\neq 0$, so it is not a cusp form.

steps: Take a [modular form](c:modular-form) $f$ for a congruence subgroup.
Expand $f$ at each cusp as a q-expansion.
If every constant term is zero, then $f$ is a cusp form.
links.why: It shows that cusp forms are the modular forms that vanish at the cusps, so they form a subspace of all modular forms.

reminder: A distribution is a continuous linear functional on smooth test functions with compact support.
definition: A distribution on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $T$ on the space of [test functions](c:test-function), the [smooth functions](c:smooth-function) with [compact support](c:compact-support) in $\Omega$, that is continuous for the usual topology of this [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space). Equivalently, on each compact set $K$ there are $C$ and $m$ with $|T(\varphi)|\le C\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$ for all test functions $\varphi$ supported in $K$.
examples: Every locally integrable function $f$ gives the distribution $\varphi\mapsto\int f\varphi\,dx$.
The [Dirac distribution](c:dirac-distribution) $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ is a distribution that no function defines.
Non-example: $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(0)^2$ is not linear, so it is not a distribution.

steps: Take a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f$ on $\Omega$.
Define $T_f(\varphi)=\int f\varphi\,dx$ for each test function $\varphi$; this map is linear and continuous.
Different smooth functions give different distributions, so every smooth function is a distribution.
links.why: It shows that distributions extend functions, so you can differentiate objects that have no derivative as functions.

steps: Take a point $a\in\Omega$ and put $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$.
This map is linear, and $|\delta_a(\varphi)|\le\sup|\varphi|$, so it is continuous.
So $\delta_a$ is a distribution of order 0 that no function defines.
links.why: It shows that point masses are distributions, which gives a first example outside the functions.

reminder: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the real vector space of $n$-tuples with the dot product and the distance it gives.
definition: Euclidean space of dimension $n$ is the [vector space](c:vector-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ over the [real numbers](c:real-number) with the standard [inner product](c:inner-product-space) $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_iy_i$. Its norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ gives the distance $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
examples: The line $\mathbb{R}$, the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ordinary space $\mathbb{R}^3$ are Euclidean spaces.
$\mathbb{R}^0$ is a single point.
Non-example: [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) has a form of signature $(1,3)$ that is not positive definite, so it is not Euclidean.

steps: Take $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_iy_i$.
This form is bilinear, symmetric and positive definite.
So $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a finite-dimensional real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), the model for all of them.
links.why: It shows that every finite-dimensional real inner product space looks like Euclidean space once you pick an orthonormal basis.

steps: Put $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The function $d$ is symmetric and positive definite, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives the triangle inequality.
So $(\mathbb{R}^n,d)$ is a [metric space](c:metric-space).
links.why: It shows that Euclidean space carries a metric, so results on metric spaces apply to it.

reminder: The Euler characteristic of a space is the alternating sum of its Betti numbers.
definition: For a space $X$ whose [homology](c:homology) groups have finite rank, the Euler characteristic is $\chi(X)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k b_k$, the alternating sum of its [Betti numbers](c:betti-number) $b_k=\operatorname{rank}H_k(X)$. For a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex), it equals $V-E+F-\cdots$, the alternating count of the simplices of each dimension.
examples: A convex polyhedron has $V-E+F=2$, so its Euler characteristic is $2$, as for the sphere.
The torus and the circle have Euler characteristic $0$, and a point has Euler characteristic $1$.
Non-example: an infinite discrete set has no Euler characteristic, because its group $H_0$ has infinite rank.

steps: Take a space $X$ and view it as an orbifold with trivial isotropy at every point.
Each cell $\sigma$ then contributes $(-1)^{\dim\sigma}/1$ to the [orbifold Euler characteristic](c:orbifold-euler-characteristic).
The sum is the ordinary Euler characteristic, so the orbifold version extends it to spaces with finite symmetries.
links.why: It shows that the ordinary Euler characteristic is the orbifold one without symmetries.

reminder: A filter is a nonempty family of subsets that is closed under supersets and finite intersections and excludes the empty set.
definition: A filter on a set $X$ is a nonempty family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $X$ such that $\emptyset\notin\mathcal F$, every superset of a member of $\mathcal F$ is in $\mathcal F$, and the intersection of two members is a member. In order theory, a filter of a [partial order](c:partial-order) is a nonempty upward closed subset in which any two members have a common lower bound in the subset; a filter on $X$ is such a filter of the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$ that omits $\emptyset$.
examples: The neighbourhood filter of a point $x$ in a topological space consists of all sets that contain an open set around $x$.
The cofinite subsets of an infinite set form a filter.
Non-example: the family of infinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is not a filter. The even numbers and the odd numbers are in it, but their intersection is empty.

steps: An [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) on $X$ is a filter $\mathcal U$ such that for each subset $A$, either $A\in\mathcal U$ or $X\setminus A\in\mathcal U$.
This condition makes $\mathcal U$ a maximal filter.
Dropping it leaves only a filter, so every ultrafilter is a filter, and Zorn's lemma extends every filter to an ultrafilter.
links.why: It shows that ultrafilters are the maximal filters, so filter facts apply to them.

steps: Take a metric space $X$.
A [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter) on $X$ is a filter that contains a set of diameter below $\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
Dropping the smallness condition leaves only a filter, so a Cauchy filter is a filter with an extra condition.
links.why: It shows that Cauchy filters are the filters that mimic Cauchy sequences, so filter tools carry over to completeness.

reminder: A free group on a set $S$ is a group generated by $S$ with no relations except the group axioms.
definition: The free group $F(S)$ on a set $S$ is the [group](c:group) of [reduced words](c:reduced-word) in the letters $s$ and $s^{-1}$ for $s\in S$, multiplied by concatenation and then cancelling each adjacent pair $ss^{-1}$ or $s^{-1}s$. It has this [universal property](c:universal-property): every map from $S$ to a group $G$ extends in exactly one way to a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $F(S)\to G$.
examples: $F(\{a\})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, the infinite cyclic group.
$F(\{a,b\})$ consists of the reduced words in $a,b,a^{-1},b^{-1}$, such as $abab^{-1}$, and it contains a free subgroup of every countable rank.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is not free. It is generated by two elements $a,b$, but they satisfy the relation $ab=ba$.

steps: In the category of groups, take the forgetful functor to sets.
A [free object](c:free-object) on $S$ is a group $F$ with a map $S\to F$ through which each map to a group factors uniquely.
The group $F(S)$ with $s\mapsto s$ has this property, so it is the free object on $S$ in groups.
links.why: It shows that free groups are one case of the free-object construction, as free modules and free algebras are other cases.

steps: Take a family of copies of the infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$, one for each $s\in S$.
Their [free product](c:free-product) is the group of reduced words in the generators and their inverses.
This group is the free group $F(S)$, so free groups are free products of copies of $\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: It shows that free groups follow from free products and that their subgroup structure can be studied the same way.

reminder: A geodesic is a curve with zero covariant acceleration, and short pieces of it are the shortest paths.
definition: In a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) a geodesic is a [curve](c:curve) $\gamma$ with $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, where $\nabla$ is the Levi-Civita [covariant derivative](c:covariant-derivative). Such a curve has constant speed, and a short enough piece of it is the shortest curve between its end points.
examples: The straight lines $t\mapsto p+tv$ with constant speed are the geodesics of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The great circles of a sphere, run at constant speed, are its geodesics.
Non-example: a circle of latitude other than the equator is not a geodesic of the sphere. Its covariant acceleration is not zero, and the great circle arc between two of its points is shorter.

steps: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric, all Christoffel symbols are zero.
The geodesic equation becomes $\ddot\gamma=0$.
Its solutions are $\gamma(t)=p+tv$, the [straight lines](c:straight-line) with constant speed.
links.why: It shows that geodesics are the curved-space version of straight lines.

reminder: A Gödel numbering gives each formula and proof its own natural number in a way that a program can compute.
definition: A Gödel numbering of a formal language, such as that of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), is an [injective](c:injection) map from its symbols, [formulas](c:formula) and finite lists of formulas (so proofs) to the [natural numbers](c:natural-number). A program can compute the number of any expression, and it can decide whether a number codes an expression.
examples: Give each symbol a number $c_i$ and code the string $s_1\dots s_k$ as $2^{c_1}3^{c_2}\cdots p_k^{c_k}$; unique prime factorization makes decoding possible.
Gödel's original numbering of the formulas of arithmetic let him build a sentence that speaks about its own provability.
Non-example: assigning to each formula the number of its symbols is not a Gödel numbering, because many different formulas get the same number.

steps: Take the set of all formulas and proofs of a formal language.
Choose an [injection](c:injection) from this set to the natural numbers, so that different expressions get different numbers.
Add the condition that coding and decoding are computable; the injection is then a Gödel numbering.
links.why: It shows that a Gödel numbering is an injection with computability conditions, so injectivity gives unique decoding.

reminder: A polynomial is irreducible when it is not constant and is not a product of two nonconstant polynomials.
definition: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$ in the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x]$ over a field or integral domain $R$ is irreducible when $f$ is nonzero and not a [unit](c:unit), and $f=gh$ implies that $g$ or $h$ is a unit. Over a field, this means that $f$ is nonconstant and is not a product of two polynomials of lower degree.
examples: $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$, but it factors as $(x-i)(x+i)$ over $\mathbb{C}$.
$x^2-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, and every polynomial of degree 1 over a field is irreducible.
Non-example: $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is reducible over every field.

steps: An [irreducible element](c:irreducible) of a ring is a nonzero nonunit that is not a product of two nonunits.
Apply this definition to the ring $R[x]$ of polynomials over a field or integral domain $R$.
The irreducible elements of $R[x]$ are exactly the irreducible polynomials.
links.why: It shows that facts on irreducible elements, such as unique factorization over a field, apply to polynomials.

reminder: A manifold is a Hausdorff second-countable space in which every point has a neighbourhood that looks like $\mathbb{R}^n$.
definition: A manifold of dimension $n$ is a [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space), second-countable [topological space](c:topological-space) $M$ in which every point has a [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to an open subset of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$. Such a homeomorphism is a chart.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ and each of its open subsets are manifolds.
The sphere $S^n$ and the torus are manifolds.
Non-example: a figure eight (two circles that meet at a point) is not a manifold, because no neighbourhood of the crossing point looks like an interval.
Non-example: the line with two origins is locally Euclidean, but it is not Hausdorff.

steps: Start with a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$.
Require that $X$ is Hausdorff and second-countable.
Require that every point has a neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$; then $X$ is a manifold.
links.why: It shows that a manifold is a topological space with local and global conditions, so general topology applies to it.

steps: A [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) is a manifold with an atlas whose transition maps are smooth.
Forget the atlas and keep only the underlying topological space $M$.
The space $M$ is a manifold, so every smooth manifold is a manifold.
links.why: It shows that smooth manifolds are manifolds with extra structure, so topological results apply to them.

steps: Take a [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$.
Every point of $M$ has a neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
So $M$ is a manifold with dimension $n=3$.
links.why: It shows that 3-manifolds are the case $n=3$ of the general definition.

reminder: A norm gives each vector a length that is positive for nonzero vectors, scales with scalars and obeys the triangle inequality.
definition: A norm on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over the [real numbers](c:real-number) or the complex numbers is a function $\|\cdot\|:V\to[0,\infty)$ with $\|v\|=0$ only for $v=0$, with $\|cv\|=|c|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $c$, and with $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$. Here $|c|$ is the [absolute value](c:absolute-value) of the scalar $c$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the formulas $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}$, $\|x\|_1=\sum|x_i|$ and $\|x\|_\infty=\max|x_i|$ are norms.
On the continuous functions on $[0,1]$, the supremum $\sup|f|$ is a norm.
Non-example: $x\mapsto|x_1|$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a seminorm but not a norm, because it is zero at $(0,1)$.
Non-example: $p(x)=\sqrt{|x_1|}+\sqrt{|x_2|}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a norm, because $p(2x)=\sqrt2\,p(x)$ instead of $2p(x)$.

steps: A [seminorm](c:seminorm) satisfies homogeneity and the triangle inequality, but it may vanish at nonzero vectors.
Take a seminorm $p$ on $V$.
Add the condition that $p(v)=0$ only for $v=0$; then $p$ is a norm.
links.why: It shows that a norm is a seminorm that separates points, so seminorm facts apply to it.

steps: Take the real line as a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$.
The [absolute value](c:absolute-value) satisfies $|cx|=|c||x|$, $|x|=0$ only for $x=0$, and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$.
These are the norm axioms, so the absolute value is the norm in dimension one.
links.why: It shows that a norm extends the absolute value from numbers to vectors.

reminder: A partial function is partial computable when some algorithm computes its value where it is defined and runs forever elsewhere.
definition: A [partial function](c:partial-function) $f$ from tuples of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) to natural numbers is partial computable when some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) halts on the input $(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ with the output $f(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ exactly when $f$ is defined there. On all other inputs, the machine never halts.
examples: Every total computable function, such as addition, is partial computable.
The square root function that is defined only on perfect squares is partial computable: search $m=0,1,2,\dots$ for an $m$ with $m^2=n$, and the search stops exactly when $n$ is a square.
Non-example: the halting function $h(e,x)$, which is $1$ if program $e$ halts on input $x$ and $0$ otherwise, is total but not partial computable.

steps: Take a total [computable function](c:computable-function) $f$, computed by a machine that halts on every input.
The same machine computes $f$ as a partial function whose domain is all of $\mathbb{N}^k$.
So $f$ is partial computable, and the total computable functions are the partial computable ones with full domain.
links.why: It shows that partial computable functions include the computable functions, and that the extra freedom is the possibility of not halting.

steps: Take a [partial function](c:partial-function) $f$ on tuples of natural numbers.
Add the condition that a Turing machine computes it: the machine halts with output $f(n)$ where $f(n)$ is defined, and runs forever elsewhere.
Then $f$ is partial computable.
links.why: It shows that partial computability is a condition on a partial function.

reminder: In a projective plane, two points lie on one line and two lines meet in one point.
definition: A projective plane is a [set](c:set) of points and a set of [lines](c:line) with an incidence relation such that any two distinct points lie on exactly one line, any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point, and there are four points with no three on a line. The last condition excludes degenerate cases.
examples: The [real projective plane](c:real-projective-plane): its points are the lines through the origin of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and its lines are the planes through the origin.
The [Fano plane](c:fano-plane) has 7 points and 7 lines, with 3 points on each line.
Non-example: the Euclidean plane is not a projective plane, because two parallel lines have no common point.

steps: Take as points the lines through the origin of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and as lines the planes through the origin.
Two distinct points span exactly one plane, and two distinct planes meet in exactly one line.
The four points spanned by $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_1+e_2+e_3$ have no three in one plane, so this is a projective plane.
links.why: It shows that the real projective plane is one model of the axioms, and it gives a way to build others.

steps: Repeat the construction of the real projective plane with the field $\mathbb{F}_2$ in place of $\mathbb{R}$.
The result has 7 points and 7 lines, with 3 points on each line.
The axioms hold over every field, so the [Fano plane](c:fano-plane) is a projective plane.
links.why: It shows that projective planes can be finite, and that the Fano plane is the smallest one.

reminder: A map is proper when it is continuous and the preimage of every compact set is compact.
definition: A [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$ between topological spaces is proper when $f^{-1}(K)$ is [compact](c:compact-space) for every compact set $K\subseteq Y$. In algebraic geometry, a morphism is proper when it is separated, of finite type and universally closed.
examples: The inclusion of a closed subset is a proper map.
Every continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is proper.
Non-example: the inclusion $(0,1)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is not proper, because the preimage of the compact set $[0,1]$ is $(0,1)$, which is not compact.

steps: Take a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$.
Add the condition that the preimage of every compact subset of $Y$ is compact.
Continuous functions with this condition are the proper maps.
links.why: It shows that properness is a compactness condition added to continuity, so continuity facts apply to proper maps.

steps: Let $X$ be a space and $p:X\to\{*\}$ the map to a point.
The compact subsets of a point are $\emptyset$ and $\{*\}$, with preimages $\emptyset$ and $X$.
So $p$ is proper exactly when $X$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
links.why: It shows that properness is compactness of $X$ relative to $Y$.

reminder: A reductive group is a linear algebraic group whose unipotent radical is trivial.
definition: A smooth connected [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) $G$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ is reductive when its unipotent radical is trivial. The unipotent radical is the largest connected unipotent [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$ over an [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) of $k$.
examples: The groups $GL_n$, $SL_n$, $Sp_{2n}$ and $SO_n$ are reductive.
Every algebraic torus is reductive.
Non-example: the group $B$ of invertible upper triangular $2\times2$ matrices is not reductive. Its unipotent radical is the nontrivial group of upper unitriangular matrices.

steps: Take a smooth connected [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) $G$ over $k$.
Form its unipotent radical over an algebraic closure of $k$.
Require this radical to be trivial; then $G$ is reductive.
links.why: It shows that reductive groups are the linear algebraic groups with no unipotent part, so general facts on linear algebraic groups apply.

steps: Take a [split reductive group](c:split-reductive-group) $G$ over $k$, which has a maximal torus that is isomorphic over $k$ to a product of copies of $\mathbb{G}_m$.
It is a reductive group, because its unipotent radical is trivial.
Dropping the splitting condition gives all reductive groups, including non-split forms such as the circle group over $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: It shows that split reductive groups are the best-behaved reductive groups, and that reductive groups are broader.

steps: Take $G=GL_n$ and a connected normal unipotent subgroup $U$ of $G$ over an algebraic closure $\bar k$.
By Kolchin's theorem, the fixed space $W$ of $U$ in $\bar k^{\,n}$ is not zero.
Since $U$ is normal, $W$ is stable under $GL_n(\bar k)$, so $W=\bar k^{\,n}$ and $U$ is trivial.
links.why: It shows that the general linear group is reductive, which makes it the first example to test statements about reductive groups.

reminder: The Ricci curvature is a symmetric tensor that comes from tracing the Riemann curvature tensor.
definition: On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with [Riemann curvature](c:riemann-curvature) tensor $R$, the Ricci curvature is the symmetric 2-tensor $\operatorname{Ric}(Y,Z)=\operatorname{tr}\big(X\mapsto R(X,Y)Z\big)$. For a unit vector $v$, the value $\operatorname{Ric}(v,v)$ is the sum of the [sectional curvatures](c:sectional-curvature) of the planes that $v$ spans with each vector of an orthonormal basis of $v^\perp$.
examples: On the round unit sphere $S^n$ the Ricci curvature is $(n-1)g$.
On flat $\mathbb{R}^n$ the Ricci curvature is $0$.
On a surface the Ricci curvature is $Kg$, where $K$ is the [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature).
Non-example: the scalar curvature is not the Ricci curvature. It is one number at each point, the trace of the Ricci tensor, not a tensor.

steps: Take a Riemannian surface; its curvature tensor is $R(X,Y)Z=K\big(\langle Y,Z\rangle X-\langle X,Z\rangle Y\big)$ with [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) $K$.
Trace over $X$ in dimension 2 to get $\operatorname{Ric}(Y,Z)=K\langle Y,Z\rangle$.
So $\operatorname{Ric}=Kg$, and the Ricci curvature of a surface is its Gaussian curvature times the metric.
links.why: It shows that Ricci curvature extends Gaussian curvature to all dimensions.

reminder: A Riemann surface is a connected one-dimensional complex manifold.
definition: A Riemann surface is a [connected](c:connected-space) [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of complex dimension 1: a connected Hausdorff space covered by charts to open subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ whose transition maps are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function).
examples: The complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ and the open unit disc are Riemann surfaces.
The [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere) $\mathbb{CP}^1$ and every complex torus $\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+\tau\mathbb{Z})$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$ are Riemann surfaces.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}^2$ is a complex manifold, but it has complex dimension 2, so it is not a Riemann surface.

steps: Take a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $M$ with charts to open subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Require $n=1$, so that every chart goes to an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$.
Require that $M$ is connected; then $M$ is a Riemann surface.
links.why: It shows that a Riemann surface is a complex manifold of dimension one, so complex manifold results apply.

steps: A [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) is a connected one-dimensional complex manifold.
Its underlying space is also compact.
Dropping compactness leaves exactly the definition of a Riemann surface.
links.why: It shows that compact Riemann surfaces are Riemann surfaces with one added topological condition.

reminder: A smooth function has continuous derivatives of every order.
definition: A function $f$ on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth when all its partial [derivatives](c:derivative) of all orders exist and are [continuous](c:continuous-function). Smooth functions are also called $C^\infty$ functions.
examples: Polynomials, $e^x$ and $\sin x$ are smooth.
The function $f(x)=e^{-1/x}$ for $x>0$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x\le0$ is smooth, but it is not [analytic](c:analytic-function) at $0$.
Non-example: $f(x)=x|x|$ is not smooth. Its first derivative $2|x|$ is continuous, but its second derivative $2\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ jumps at $0$.

steps: Start with a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f$ on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Ask that the first partial derivatives exist and are continuous, then the second ones, and so on.
Functions with all these derivatives continuous are smooth.
links.why: It shows that smoothness is continuity of $f$ and of all its derivatives.

steps: Take an [analytic function](c:analytic-function) $f$, given near each point by a convergent power series.
A convergent power series can be differentiated term by term any number of times.
So all derivatives of $f$ exist and are continuous, and $f$ is smooth.
links.why: It shows that every analytic function is smooth, but the function $e^{-1/x}$ shows the converse fails.

steps: A [bump function](c:bump-function) is a smooth function with compact support.
Forget the support condition and keep only the smoothness.
Every bump function is then a smooth function, and a smooth function may fail to vanish outside every compact set.
links.why: It shows that bump functions are the smooth functions that you can localize, which is why they cut smooth data down to small regions.

reminder: A stopping time is a random time $\tau$ such that you can tell whether $\tau\le t$ from the information up to time $t$.
definition: Let $(\mathcal F_t)$ be a [filtration](c:filtration) on a probability space. A stopping time is a [random variable](c:random-variable) $\tau$ with values in $[0,\infty]$ such that $\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t\ge0$. In discrete time, this means that $\{\tau=n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$.
examples: Every constant time $\tau=c$ is a stopping time.
In discrete time, the first $n$ with $X_n\in B$, for an adapted process $(X_n)$ and a [Borel set](c:borel-set) $B$, is a stopping time.
Non-example: the last time before $N$ at which a random walk is at $0$ is not a stopping time, because to decide that the time is $n$ you must know that the walk does not return to $0$ later.

steps: Take a stopping time $\tau$ for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_t)$.
For each $t$, the event $\{\tau\le t\}$ lies in $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F$.
So $\tau$ is measurable for $\mathcal F$, and hence a [random variable](c:random-variable) with values in $[0,\infty]$.
The extra condition is that each event $\{\tau\le t\}$ lies in the smaller sigma-algebra $\mathcal F_t$.
links.why: It shows that a stopping time is a random variable that respects the flow of information.

reminder: A Sylow $p$-subgroup of a finite group is a subgroup whose order is the largest power of $p$ that divides the group order.
definition: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $p$ a [prime number](c:prime-number), and write $|G|=p^am$ with $p\nmid m$. A Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of [order](c:order-of-a-group) $p^a$.
examples: In $S_3$ the subgroup $\{e,(12)\}$ is a Sylow 2-subgroup, and $\{e,(123),(132)\}$ is the Sylow 3-subgroup.
In $\mathbb{Z}/12$ the subgroup $\{0,3,6,9\}$ is the Sylow 2-subgroup, and $\{0,4,8\}$ is the Sylow 3-subgroup.
Non-example: in $S_4$, which has order 24, the subgroup $\{e,(12)\}$ has order 2. It is a 2-subgroup but not a Sylow 2-subgroup, because the Sylow 2-subgroups have order 8.

steps: Take a finite group $G$ and a prime $p$ with $|G|=p^am$ and $p\nmid m$.
Choose a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $P\le G$.
Require $|P|=p^a$; then $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup.
links.why: It shows that Sylow subgroups are subgroups of a prescribed order, so Lagrange's theorem applies to them.

steps: A [p-group](c:p-group) is a group whose order is a power of $p$.
A Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ has order $p^a$, so $P$ is a $p$-group.
By Lagrange's theorem, every $p$-subgroup of $G$ has order at most $p^a$, so no $p$-subgroup is larger than $P$.
links.why: It shows that a Sylow subgroup is a $p$-group of the largest possible size.

reminder: A uniform distribution spreads probability evenly: equal outcomes are equally likely, or the density is constant.
definition: A uniform distribution is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) in which each outcome of a finite set $S$ has probability $1/|S|$. On an interval $[a,b]$, it is the distribution with constant [density](c:probability-density-function) $1/(b-a)$, so the probability of a subinterval is its length divided by $b-a$.
examples: A fair die gives probability $1/6$ to each of the numbers $1,\dots,6$.
A random number $X$ drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$ satisfies $P(X\le x)=x$.
Non-example: the sum of two fair dice is not uniform on $\{2,\dots,12\}$, because $7$ has probability $1/6$ and $2$ has probability $1/36$.

steps: Take a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on a finite set or on an interval of finite length.
Require that the probability of every part depends only on its size, which is its count or its length.
Then the distribution is uniform, with constant point mass or constant density.
links.why: It shows that the uniform distribution is the distribution with no preferred outcomes.

reminder: A subset of a complex manifold is analytic when, near every point, it is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions.
definition: A subset $A$ of a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $M$ is an analytic set when every point $p\in M$ has an open [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ and finitely many [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) $f_1,\dots,f_k$ on $U$ with $A\cap U=\{z\in U: f_1(z)=\dots=f_k(z)=0\}$. Such a set is closed in $M$.
examples: A closed complex submanifold, such as $\{z_n=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^n$, is an analytic set.
The cuspidal curve $\{z_1^2=z_2^3\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ is an analytic set with a singular point at the origin.

Non-example: the closed unit disc in $\mathbb{C}$ is not an analytic set. A holomorphic function that vanishes on an open piece of the disc near a boundary point vanishes on a whole connected neighbourhood, by the identity theorem.

steps: Take a point $p\in M$ outside the analytic set $A$, and choose $U$ and $f_1,\dots,f_k$ as in the definition.
Since $p\notin A\cap U$, some $f_i(p)$ is not zero.
By continuity, $f_i\neq0$ near $p$, so a neighbourhood of $p$ misses $A$, and $A$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set).
links.why: It shows that analytic sets are closed, and that they are the closed sets with a local holomorphic equation.

steps: Take an analytic set $A$ in $M$ and the sheaf $\mathcal I$ of holomorphic functions that vanish on $A$.
The quotient sheaf $\mathcal O_M/\mathcal I$ restricted to $A$ makes $A$ a ringed space.
Locally this space is the zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, so $A$ is a reduced [complex analytic space](c:complex-analytic-space).
links.why: It shows that analytic sets are the reduced complex analytic spaces that sit inside a complex manifold.

reminder: A bipartite graph has its vertices split into two sets so that every edge joins one set to the other.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ is bipartite when its [vertex](c:vertex) set splits as $V=A\cup B$ with $A\cap B=\emptyset$ so that every [edge](c:edge) has one end in $A$ and one end in $B$. Equivalently, $G$ has no cycle of odd length.
examples: The complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ is bipartite, with the two parts of sizes $m$ and $n$.
Every tree and every cycle of even length is bipartite.
Non-example: a triangle is not bipartite. If $a\in A$, then its neighbour $b$ lies in $B$, then the next vertex $c$ lies in $A$, but $c$ is adjacent to $a$.

steps: Take a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$.
Look for a split $V=A\cup B$ into two disjoint sets with no edge inside $A$ or inside $B$.
If such a split exists, $G$ is a bipartite graph.
links.why: It shows that being bipartite is a property of a graph, which you can test by finding the two sides.

steps: A [tree](c:tree) is a connected graph with no cycle; pick a root vertex $r$.
Put each vertex in $A$ if its distance from $r$ is even, and in $B$ if its distance is odd.
Each edge joins two vertices whose distances differ by exactly 1, so it joins $A$ to $B$ and the tree is bipartite.
links.why: It shows that every tree is bipartite, so results for bipartite graphs apply to trees.

reminder: A classifying space $BG$ is a space whose homotopy classes of maps from $X$ correspond to principal $G$-bundles over $X$.
definition: For a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$, a classifying space is a space $BG$ with a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $EG\to BG$ whose total space $EG$ is [contractible](c:contractible-space). For every [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$, pulling back this bundle gives a bijection from the set $[X,BG]$ of [homotopy classes](c:homotopy-class) of maps to the isomorphism classes of principal $G$-bundles over $X$.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$, the classifying space is $\mathbb{RP}^\infty$.
For $G=U(1)$, the classifying space is $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$.

Non-example: a point is not a classifying space of $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$. Pulling back along the one map from $S^1$ to a point gives only the trivial bundle, but $\mathbb{Z}/2$-bundles over $S^1$ include the nontrivial double cover.

steps: Take $G=U(n)$, the unitary group, which is a topological group.
A principal $U(n)$-bundle is the same as a complex vector bundle of rank $n$.
The classifying space $BG$ is then [BU(n)](c:bu-n), and $[X,BU(n)]$ classifies complex vector bundles of rank $n$ over $X$.
links.why: It shows that BU(n) is the classifying space for rank $n$ complex vector bundles, so general facts on classifying spaces apply.

steps: Take $G=O(n)$, the orthogonal group, which is a topological group.
A principal $O(n)$-bundle is the same as a real vector bundle of rank $n$.
The classifying space $BG$ is then [BO(n)](c:bo-n), and $[X,BO(n)]$ classifies real vector bundles of rank $n$ over $X$.
links.why: It shows that BO(n) is the classifying space for rank $n$ real vector bundles, so characteristic classes live in its cohomology.

reminder: Cohomology turns a cochain complex into abelian groups of cocycles modulo coboundaries.
definition: For a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) $(C^\bullet,d)$ of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) with $d\circ d=0$, the $n$-th cohomology group is $H^n=\ker(d:C^n\to C^{n+1})/\operatorname{im}(d:C^{n-1}\to C^n)$. For a space or an algebraic object, one applies this to a cochain complex built from it, and the result is contravariant and dual to [homology](c:homology).
examples: The de Rham cohomology of a manifold is the cohomology of the differential forms with the exterior derivative.
The singular cohomology of a point has $H^0=\mathbb{Z}$ and $H^n=0$ for $n>0$.
Non-example: for maps $d:C^n\to C^{n+1}$ with $d\circ d\neq0$, the quotient $\ker d/\operatorname{im}d$ is not defined, because the image need not lie in the kernel.

steps: Take the cochain complex $\Omega^\bullet(M)$ of differential forms on a smooth manifold $M$ with the exterior derivative $d$.
It satisfies $d\circ d=0$, so it is a cochain complex of real vector spaces.
Its cohomology is the [de Rham cohomology](c:de-rham-cohomology) of $M$.
links.why: It shows that de Rham cohomology is cohomology of one specific cochain complex.

steps: Take a group $G$, a $G$-module $A$ and a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to\mathbb{Z}$ over $\mathbb{Z}[G]$.
Form the cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_G(P_\bullet,A)$.
Its cohomology is $H^n(G,A)$, the [group cohomology](c:group-cohomology) of $G$ with coefficients in $A$.
links.why: It shows that group cohomology is cohomology of a Hom complex, so general cohomology tools apply.

steps: Take a sheaf $F$ of abelian groups on a space $X$ and an injective resolution $I^\bullet$ of $F$.
Apply the global sections functor to get the cochain complex $I^\bullet(X)$.
Its cohomology is the [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) $H^n(X,F)$.
links.why: It shows that sheaf cohomology is cohomology of a global sections complex, so long exact sequences carry over.

reminder: A compact group is a topological group whose underlying space is compact and Hausdorff.
definition: A compact group is a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$ whose underlying space is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space). Such a group has a unique invariant probability measure, the [Haar measure](c:haar-measure).
examples: Every finite group with the discrete topology is a compact group.
The circle group $U(1)$ and the groups $SU(n)$ and $O(n)$ are compact groups.
Non-example: the group $(\mathbb{R},+)$ is a topological group but is not compact, because the cover by the intervals $(-n,n)$ has no finite subcover.

steps: Take a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$.
Require that the underlying space of $G$ is compact.
Require that it is Hausdorff; then $G$ is a compact group.
links.why: It shows that a compact group is a topological group with a compactness condition, so general topological group facts apply.

steps: Give a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ the discrete topology.
Every map out of a discrete space is continuous, so multiplication and inversion are continuous.
A finite discrete space is compact and Hausdorff, so $G$ is a compact group.
links.why: It shows that every finite group is a compact group, so compact group results hold for finite groups.

steps: A [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group) is a Lie group whose underlying space is compact.
A Lie group is a topological group, and its underlying manifold is Hausdorff.
So a compact Lie group is a topological group whose space is compact Hausdorff, which is a compact group.
links.why: It shows that compact Lie groups are the compact groups that are also smooth manifolds.

reminder: A compact metric space is a metric space in which every sequence has a convergent subsequence.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is compact when every [sequence](c:sequence) in $X$ has a convergent [subsequence](c:subsequence) whose limit lies in $X$. Equivalently, $X$ is a [compact space](c:compact-space) in its metric topology, or $X$ is complete and totally bounded.
examples: Every closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ is a compact metric space, and so is every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Heine-Borel).
The Cantor set and the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ are compact metric spaces.
Non-example: $(0,1)$ with the usual metric is not compact, because the sequence $1/n$ has no subsequence that converges in $(0,1)$.

steps: Take a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$.
Require that every sequence in $X$ has a subsequence that converges in $X$.
Metric spaces with this property are the compact metric spaces.
links.why: It shows that compactness is a condition on a metric space, and that you can test it with sequences.

steps: Take a [compact space](c:compact-space) $X$ whose topology comes from a metric $d$.
In a metric space, compactness by open covers is equivalent to compactness by sequences.
So $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space, and every compact space with a metric topology is one.
links.why: It shows that compact metric spaces have all the properties of compact spaces, such as the extreme value theorem.

reminder: A compact operator maps every bounded set to a set whose closure is compact.
definition: A linear operator $T:X\to Y$ between [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) is compact when it maps every [bounded set](c:bounded-set) of $X$ to a [relatively compact](c:relatively-compact-subspace) subset of $Y$. Equivalently, for every bounded sequence $(x_n)$, the sequence $(Tx_n)$ has a convergent subsequence.
examples: Every bounded linear operator of finite rank is compact, for example $x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle v$.
The integral operator $(Tf)(x)=\int_0^1K(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ with $K$ continuous on $[0,1]^2$ is a compact operator on $C[0,1]$.
Non-example: the identity operator on an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact, because its unit ball is not relatively compact (Riesz lemma).

steps: Take a compact operator $T:X\to Y$ and the unit ball $B$ of $X$.
The image $T(B)$ is relatively compact, hence bounded.
So $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C$, and $T$ is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) with a stronger property.
links.why: It shows that every compact operator is bounded, so results on bounded operators apply.

steps: A [trace class operator](c:trace-class-operator) on a Hilbert space has singular values $s_n$ with $\sum s_n<\infty$.
Convergence of this series forces the singular values $s_n$ to tend to $0$.
An operator whose singular values tend to $0$ is a norm limit of finite-rank operators, so it is compact.
links.why: It shows that trace class operators are compact, so spectral theory of compact operators applies to them.

reminder: A complex manifold is a space covered by charts to open sets of $\mathbb{C}^n$ whose transition maps are holomorphic.
definition: A complex manifold of dimension $n$ is a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ with an [atlas](c:atlas) of charts $\varphi_i:U_i\to\mathbb{C}^n$ onto open subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$ whose transition maps $\varphi_j\circ\varphi_i^{-1}$ are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function). Since $\mathbb{C}^n\cong\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, the space $M$ is also a manifold of real dimension $2n$.
examples: The space $\mathbb{C}^n$ and each of its open subsets are complex manifolds.
The complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$, with charts that divide by one coordinate, is a complex manifold.
Non-example: the 3-sphere $S^3$ is not a complex manifold, because its real dimension is odd and a complex manifold has real dimension $2n$.

steps: Identify $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$.
A holomorphic map between open subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$ is a smooth map between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$.
So the transition maps are smooth, the atlas is a smooth atlas, and $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) of dimension $2n$.
links.why: It shows that every complex manifold is a smooth manifold of even dimension, so smooth tools apply to it.

steps: A [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) is a connected complex manifold with complex dimension 1.
Its charts go to open subsets of $\mathbb{C}$, and its transition maps are holomorphic.
So it is a complex manifold with $n=1$ and an added connectedness condition.
links.why: It shows that Riemann surfaces are the one-dimensional case, where the theory of complex manifolds is richest.

steps: A [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) is a complex manifold $M$ with a Hermitian metric.
The metric has a closed fundamental 2-form, which is the extra condition.
Forget the metric and keep the holomorphic atlas; $M$ is still a complex manifold.
links.why: It shows that Kähler manifolds are complex manifolds with a compatible metric, so complex manifold results apply.

reminder: A conic section is a plane curve that a plane cuts from a double cone.
definition: A nondegenerate conic section is the curve where a plane that misses the apex cuts a double circular [cone](c:cone). It is an ellipse (a [circle](c:circle) when the plane is perpendicular to the axis), a parabola or a hyperbola. Apart from degenerate cases, it is the zero set of one [polynomial](c:polynomial) $ax^2+bxy+cy^2+dx+ey+f$ of degree two.
examples: The unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$ is a conic section.
The parabola $y=x^2$ and the [hyperbola](c:hyperbola) $xy=1$ are conic sections.
Non-example: the cubic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ has degree three, so it is not a conic section; it is an elliptic curve.

steps: An [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) is the zero set of a polynomial in two variables.
A conic section is the zero set of a polynomial of degree two.
So conic sections are the plane algebraic curves of degree two, and results such as Bézout's theorem apply.
links.why: It shows that conics are the degree-two case of plane algebraic curves.

steps: Take a double cone with the $z$-axis as its axis, and a plane perpendicular to the axis that misses the apex.
By symmetry about the axis, the section is a [circle](c:circle).
Tilting the plane gives ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas, so the circle is a conic section.
links.why: It shows that the circle is the simplest conic section, and that the other conics come from tilting the plane.

reminder: A covering map is a continuous surjection in which each point has a neighbourhood whose preimage splits into copies of it.
definition: A [continuous](c:continuous-function) [surjection](c:surjection) $p:E\to X$ of topological spaces is a covering map when every $x\in X$ has an open [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ such that $p^{-1}(U)$ is a [disjoint union](c:disjoint-union) of open sets, each mapped by $p$ [homeomorphically](c:homeomorphism) onto $U$. Then $E$ is a covering space of $X$.
examples: The map $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$, is a covering map.
The quotient map $S^n\to\mathbb{RP}^n$, which identifies antipodal points, is a covering map.
Non-example: the map $(0,2)\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}$, is not a covering map. Over a small arc around $1$, the piece $(0,\varepsilon)$ maps onto only half of the arc.

steps: Take a covering map $p:E\to X$ and a point $e\in E$.
Let $U$ be an evenly covered neighbourhood of $p(e)$, and let $V$ be the open sheet of $p^{-1}(U)$ that contains $e$.
The map $p|_V:V\to U$ is a homeomorphism between open sets, so $p$ is a [local homeomorphism](c:local-homeomorphism), with the extra condition of even covering.
links.why: It shows that every covering map is a local homeomorphism, so local results apply to it.

steps: A [universal covering space](c:universal-covering-space) of $X$ is a covering space of $X$ that is simply connected.
Take a covering map $p:\tilde X\to X$ with $\tilde X$ simply connected.
Dropping the simple connectivity leaves just a covering space, and the universal one covers every other cover.
links.why: It shows that the universal cover is the largest covering space, so you can compare all covers with it.

steps: Take a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $h:E\to X$.
Every point has the neighbourhood $U=X$, and $h^{-1}(X)=E$ is one open set mapped homeomorphically onto $X$.
So $h$ is a covering map with one sheet.
links.why: It shows that homeomorphisms are the one-sheeted covering maps.
